objectives: Stage a dance with sight-line + scenography + lighting awareness.
Differentiate concert dance + Broadway + film conventions.
Brief a designer, director-of-photography or camera operator.

slides.title: Stagecraft — sight lines, lighting, costume + scenography
slides.body:
Choreography reaches an audience only through the conditions of its **presentation**. Stagecraft is the second half of the choreographer's job: design the space, the lights, the costumes, the scenography, the entrance + exit, the run order. **Twyla Tharp**'s memoir-with-notebook *The Creative Habit* (2003) emphasises the slogan 'make it move' — meaning make it move for the eye watching it, not only for the dancer doing it.

**Sight lines + stage geometry**. Most concert dance is staged on a **proscenium**: the audience sits in front of a frame + sees one face of the work. **Sight lines** are the visual rays from each seat to each part of the stage; a movement upstage centre might be invisible from a side seat (called 'in the wings' or 'masked'). Choreographer + technical director must:
- Block to keep critical moments inside the audience's visible cone.
- Avoid clustering on the stage-left or stage-right diagonals if there's a side balcony.
- Use downstage-centre for intimacy; upstage-centre for processional or revelation.
- Test from corner seats during tech rehearsal.

**Thrust** (audience on three sides) + **theatre-in-the-round** + **black-box flexible** spaces have entirely different geometries. The corps of *Swan Lake* arranged in a Petipa diagonal becomes incoherent in the round; the choreography must be rebuilt.

**Lighting design**. The lighting designer is the choreographer's closest tech collaborator. Core variables:
- **Direction** — front (flat), side (sculpts limbs — the classic dance angle), top (isolates dancer from floor), back (silhouettes), floor (uplight, theatrical).
- **Color** — gels or LED RGBA; cool blues + greens for night / abstraction; warm ambers + pinks for narrative / period.
- **Intensity + cue progression** — the cue list is the lighting score paralleling the choreography.
- **Specials** — single beams isolating a dancer or shape.
- **Cyc + scrim** — backdrops painted with light.
Key designers historically: Jean Rosenthal (Graham + Balanchine), Jennifer Tipton (Trisha Brown, Tharp, McGregor — National Medal of Arts 2008), James F. Ingalls, Robert Wierzel, Tom Visser (NDT).

**Costume**. Function (allow the vocabulary), silhouette (read at distance), period or abstraction, identification (caste / role), color contrast against scenography. Classical ballet tutus + pointe shoes are themselves costume conventions encoding a class lineage. Bausch's bias-cut silk dresses + slip dresses became part of Tanztheater identity.

**Scenography** = the full visual world of the stage: set, projection, props, floor surface, stage architecture. **Isamu Noguchi**'s sets for Martha Graham (1944-1972, including *Appalachian Spring* 1944) defined American modern scenography. **Robert Rauschenberg** designed for Cunningham + Trisha Brown; **Karole Armitage** + Jean-Paul Gaultier collaborated. Contemporary work increasingly uses **video projection** + **interactive media** (Klaus Obermaier, OpenEndedGroup with Cunningham, Random International with Wayne McGregor — P89 L8).

slides.title: Concert dance versus Broadway — Fosse, Stroman, Blankenbuehler
slides.body:
**Concert dance** = standalone artistic dance presented as the work itself: ballet, modern, contemporary, postmodern, hip-hop concert work. Auditorium settings (proscenium or thrust), single-evening programming, presenter-funded, focus on choreography-as-art-object.

**Broadway musical theatre** = dance integrated with song, dialogue, plot, set design, eight shows a week for months or years. Different demands:
- Dance must support story + character, not stand alone.
- Choreography must read instantly + multiple times (eight shows a week, every performance the same quality).
- Costume changes, set transitions, mic packs, complex staging cues — choreography lives inside this machine.
- Equity rules, replacement casts, dance captains maintaining the choreography long after the choreographer has left.
- Reduced rehearsal time per dance compared to a concert company that may rehearse a 20-min work for 6 weeks.

**Bob Fosse** (1927-1987) — the most iconic American musical-theatre choreographer-director. Unified choreography + direction (rare); won Tony + Oscar + Emmy in 1973 alone (*Pippin*, *Cabaret*, *Liza with a Z*). Major works:
- *The Pajama Game* (1954) + *Damn Yankees* (1955) early career.
- *Sweet Charity* (Broadway 1966; film 1969).
- *Cabaret* (film 1972 — Oscar).
- *Pippin* (1972 — Tony).
- *Chicago* (Broadway 1975; film 2002 by Rob Marshall preserving Fosse vocabulary).
- *All That Jazz* (1979 film — autobiographical).
Fosse style: turned-in feet, isolated shoulders, slithering sideways, derby hats, gloved hands, jazz hands → jazz fingers, broken wrists, finger snaps. The whole vocabulary recognisable in two seconds (P89 L6).

**Susan Stroman** (b.1954) — choreographer-director, defining figure of late-20C + 21C Broadway. Five-time Tony winner. *Crazy for You* (1992), *Show Boat* (1994), *Contact* (1999), *The Producers* (2001 — Tony for both choreography + direction), *Young Frankenstein* (2007), *Bullets over Broadway* (2014). Stroman blends classical-jazz + ballet vocabularies + has a particular skill for dance-as-comedy.

**Andy Blankenbuehler** (b.1970) — choreographed **Lin-Manuel Miranda's *Hamilton* (2015)** + *In the Heights* (2008, 2021 film) + *Bandstand* (2017). *Hamilton*'s choreography fused hip-hop, contemporary, jazz + ballet vocabularies + introduced a continuously moving ensemble (the Blankenbuehler 'reverse', the lift on 'Wait For It') that became a new Broadway dance vernacular. Tony, Olivier + a generational influence on musical-theatre choreography.

Other important figures: Jerome Robbins (*West Side Story* 1957, *Fiddler on the Roof* 1964), Michael Bennett (*A Chorus Line* 1975), Tommy Tune, Gillian Lynne (*Cats* + *The Phantom of the Opera*), Garth Fagan (*The Lion King* 1997), Christopher Wheeldon (*An American in Paris* 2014).

**Twyla Tharp** (b.1941) is the rare figure who works fluently in concert dance + Broadway + film. Founded the Twyla Tharp Dance company 1965; choreographed for ABT + NYCB; *Movin' Out* (Broadway 2002, Billy Joel score, Tony); film choreography for *Hair* (1979), *Amadeus* (1984), *White Nights* (1985). Tharp's slogan from *The Creative Habit* — 'make it move' — is the discipline-spanning aesthetic motto: choreography is shaped to move *the eye*, whatever the venue.

slides.title: Film dance + the camera as choreographic instrument
slides.body:
Film + television impose entirely new conditions on choreography: the camera selects + reframes the dance the audience sees; editing chops it into fragments + reassembles it; the dancer performs to a click track + playback; lighting is now film-lighting (color temperature + key + fill + rim + flag) not stage lighting.

**Classical Hollywood era**:
- **Fred Astaire** (1899-1987) + **Ginger Rogers** — RKO musicals (1933-1939). Astaire fought the studio for **full-body framing** + **long takes**: his dances were filmed in wide shot from the head to feet, edited minimally, often in single takes per number. The dance-on-film grammar he established is still the gold standard: see the whole body + see the whole phrase.
- **Gene Kelly** (1912-1996) — *Singin' in the Rain* (1952), *An American in Paris* (1951 — choreographed an 18-minute ballet finale to Gershwin). Athletic + grounded + balletic. Frequently directed his own dance sequences + integrated camera movement into the choreography.
- **Busby Berkeley** — Warner Bros 1930s. Top-down + crane-shot mass geometry; the dance is the choreography of the camera + the dancers' formations seen from impossible angles. *42nd Street* (1933), *Gold Diggers of 1933*.
- **Michael Kidd, Stanley Donen, Vincente Minnelli** as the choreographer-director generation.

**Mid-century transition**:
- **Bob Fosse** as film director — *Sweet Charity* (1969), *Cabaret* (1972), *All That Jazz* (1979). Brought Broadway dance to film with editing that shaped the dance into film phrases.
- **Saturday Night Fever** (1977) + **Flashdance** (1983) + **Footloose** (1984) — dance as pop spectacle, MTV-era cutting.

**Contemporary film dance**:
- **Justin Hurwitz / Damien Chazelle's *La La Land* (2016)** — Mandy Moore (choreographer) revived classical Hollywood single-take dance ('Another Day of Sun' on the LA freeway; 'Planetarium' at the Griffith Observatory) consciously in dialogue with Astaire + Kelly. The film's musical-direction model resurrected long-take dance for a 21C audience + signaled a craft-revival.
- ***In the Heights* (2021 film), *West Side Story* (2021 Spielberg)** — restaging classic Broadway choreography with contemporary cinematography.
- ***tick, tick... BOOM!* (2021)**, ***Mean Girls* (2024)** — Broadway-to-film pipeline staying active.
- **Dance films + dance documentaries**: Wim Wenders's *Pina* (2011, 3D) on Bausch; Frederick Wiseman's *La Danse* (2009) on Paris Opera Ballet; Wayne McGregor's *Living Archive* (2018) film-of-process with Google Arts & Culture (P89 L8).

**Music videos** are their own choreographic medium. Michael Jackson + Michael Peters (*Thriller* 1983); Janet Jackson + Paula Abdul + Tina Landon (1980s-90s); Beyoncé + JaQuel Knight (*Single Ladies* 2008); Travis Scott + Sean Bankhead. Music video reaches the largest audiences any choreographer reaches.

**Choreographer's film-craft checklist**:
1. Can you stage to a camera lens + a planned framing, not to an audience seat?
2. Can you choreograph for a click track / playback in 1-bar segments suitable for film editing?
3. Can you communicate with the director of photography about camera movement + shot length?
4. Can you make a single take that holds up, vs. one that depends on editing?
5. Can you compose for the small screen (phone) — TikTok-era constraints (P89 L8)?

The choreographer who can move between concert stage, Broadway pit + camera lens has the broadest reach. Twyla Tharp + Susan Stroman + Andy Blankenbuehler + Justin Peck (NYCB resident + *West Side Story* 2021 film) are 21C exemplars.

question.question: Stage the same 4-minute solo in four venues
question.goal: A 4-minute contemporary solo is to be performed in (a) a 2000-seat proscenium opera house; (b) a 200-seat black box; (c) a Broadway musical insert; (d) a 60-second TikTok video. Choose the staging adjustments for each.

steps.prompt: Proscenium opera house — biggest staging adjustment?

acceptedAnswers: scale up the gestures + use side lighting + reduce facial detail expectations; downstage placement

steps.reveal: Scale up. A 2000-seat house puts the back-row seat 30 m from the stage; subtle gestures + facial detail are lost. Translate intimate gestures into full-body + limb shapes; use side lighting to sculpt limbs; stay downstage where possible; let costume + silhouette do work the face would do up close. Jennifer Tipton + Robert Rauschenberg are reference designers for this scale.

acceptedAnswers: use breath + micro-gesture + eye contact; flexible audience configuration

steps.reveal: Use intimacy. The audience can hear breath + see eye contact + read facial micro-gesture; the work can include speech, whispers, a glance into the front row. Stage from multiple sides if the box is flexible. Tanztheater-style autobiographical material reads here when it wouldn't from a proscenium.

acceptedAnswers: fit the solo into 4 minutes of show that advances plot + character + can be replicated 8 times a week for months

steps.reveal: Story + sustainability. The solo must advance the character + plot + integrate with the cue list (lighting, scenery, sound, mic packs). Choreographer must teach the solo to swing dancers + replacement casts; dance captain maintains it nightly. Vocabulary should not risk injury under 8-show-a-week load. Stroman + Blankenbuehler + Fosse all designed for this constraint.

acceptedAnswers: vertical 9:16 framing; close-up upper body + face; 8-count hook that can be learned + replicated by viewers

steps.reveal: Fundamental redesign. Vertical 9:16 framing privileges upper body + face; lower body often cropped out. 60 seconds = roughly an 8-count hook + a development + a payoff. A successful TikTok dance is also a *learnable* dance — the audience replicates it; design for instructability + tagging. Charli D'Amelio's *Renegade* (2019, choreography by Jalaiah Harmon) + Brian Esperon's *WAP* (2020) are reference cases (P89 L8).

question.question: What is the defining feature of Fred Astaire's filmed dances that the 21C revival in *La La Land* (2016) deliberately referenced?
options: Full-body framing + long takes — Astaire insisted at RKO from 1933 that his dances be filmed in wide shot, framed from head to feet so the whole body was visible + with minimal editing, often in single takes per number. The grammar he established became the gold standard for filmed dance: see the whole phrase + see the whole body. Damien Chazelle + choreographer Mandy Moore deliberately revived this grammar in *La La Land* (2016) — 'Another Day of Sun' filmed in single takes on the LA freeway; 'Planetarium' at the Griffith Observatory; long-take camera moves that integrate the dance into the cinematography rather than fragmenting it. The result signaled a 21C craft-revival of classical Hollywood dance-film convention.
Use of motion-capture for the lower body.
Color cinematography contrasting with black-and-white dance sequences.
question.explanation: Astaire fought for + won full-body framing + long takes — RKO musicals from 1933 onward. The dance grammar he established (whole body + whole phrase, minimal editing) was deliberately revived by Damien Chazelle + Mandy Moore in *La La Land* (2016) — single takes on the freeway, the Griffith Observatory sequence, long camera moves through the dance.
hints: It's about the camera, not the dancer.
What does *La La Land*'s 'Another Day of Sun' have in common with Astaire?
question.workedSolution: Astaire's signature was full-body framing + long takes — at RKO from 1933 he insisted his dances be filmed in wide shot, head to feet visible, often in single takes per number. The grammar (whole body + whole phrase, minimal editing) became the gold standard for filmed dance. *La La Land* (2016, Damien Chazelle + choreographer Mandy Moore) deliberately revived this — single takes on the LA freeway ('Another Day of Sun'), long camera moves at the Griffith Observatory ('Planetarium'). A 21C craft-revival of classical Hollywood film-dance grammar.

question.question: Briefing a lighting + costume designer
question.prompt: You are making a new 25-minute contemporary ballet for 10 dancers. Music: a single Steve Reich phase-shifting score with no major dynamic peaks. The lighting designer + costume designer ask: 'How do we keep this visually alive for 25 minutes if the music has no peaks?' Brief them: how do you use color, direction + intensity in lighting + how do you use silhouette + color in costume to mark the structural sections of the dance (sections you've imposed onto the music)? Name at least one historical reference designer (Tipton, Rosenthal, Wierzel, Visser) + one structural device (canon, retrograde, accumulation — P89 L3) you are using to map onto their visual language.

question.question: A Broadway musical runs 8 shows per week for 50 weeks. Each show contains 12 minutes of dance for a 22-person ensemble. Compute the total person-minutes of dance performed across the run.

question.prompt: In ≤150 words, explain why staging + lighting + costume + camera are inseparable from choreography for the audience. Reference Twyla Tharp's 'make it move' + name one Broadway choreographer + one film choreographer.
question.rubric: Should articulate: choreography exists for the audience only through staging, lighting, costume + (for film) camera + editing. The same phrase can read as elegant or invisible depending on sight line, lighting direction (front / side / top / back) + costume silhouette. Sight lines + stage geometry (proscenium / thrust / round / black box) determine what choreographer can do upstage / centre / wings. Lighting + costume designer + scenographer are key collaborators (Jennifer Tipton, Isamu Noguchi for Graham, Rauschenberg for Cunningham + Brown). Broadway: Fosse, Susan Stroman, Andy Blankenbuehler (*Hamilton* 2015) bring dance into integrated musical theatre with story + 8-show-a-week sustainability. Film: Astaire's full-body framing + long takes are the gold standard, revived by *La La Land* (2016) under Mandy Moore + Hurwitz. Twyla Tharp's 'make it move' (2003) is the discipline-spanning aesthetic motto — choreography is shaped to move *the eye*, whatever the venue.
